failures.rule: arrays can be concatenated with arrays when only non-newline whitespace separates them
objects can be concatenated with objects when only non-newline whitespace separates them
it is an error to concatenate an array with an object
for purposes of concatenation a substitution that resolves to an array also means an array, so ${x} [ 1, 2 ] with x an array concatenates into one array
for purposes of concatenation a substitution that resolves to an object also means an object, so ${x} { c : 1 } with x an object merges into one object
for objects, concatenation means merging, and the second object overrides the first on overlapping keys
arrays cannot be field keys; nested inside an object so the rejection comes from the key position, not from the document root
objects cannot be field keys; nested inside an object so the rejection comes from the key position, not from the document root
the spec's worked example: object concatenation with a substitution is a common way to express inheritance
the spec's worked example: array concatenation with a substitution is a common way to add to paths
the spec's worked example: a later array definition can concatenate a substitution referring to its own earlier value with a new array
newlines may occur within an array without preventing it from concatenating with a second array on the same line as its closing bracket
a substitution that resolves to an object means an object for concatenation, and concatenating an object with an array is an error
a substitution that resolves to an array means an array for concatenation, and concatenating an array with an object is an error
it is an error to concatenate an object with an array in this order too, not only array then object
a newline between two arrays in a field value prevents concatenation, so the second array begins a new field, and an array cannot be a field key

an object whose field a is itself a merge of an object and a substitution concatenates with a substituted object like any other: the two merge. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) because the concatenation is not registered as the merge's parent; the same objects written as literals concatenate fine

${a} in a's own value refers to the earlier a, an object, so the concatenation merges {p: ...} with {q: 1}; the inner p is itself a merge of an object and a substitution. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) when the merge inside a concatenation piece resolves, as in 018
the spec's worked example: whitespace on the same line between two bracketed arrays concatenates them into a single element, the array [1, 2, 3, 4]
the spec's worked example: unquoted words and substitutions separated by whitespace concatenate into one string element, and only the comma separates elements

a: This is an unquoted string my name is Alice
expected.name: Alice

failures.rule: the spec's worked example: whitespace between two substitutions concatenates them into one element, and the comma separates the two concatenations
non-newline whitespace is never a field separator, so two field definitions cannot be written on one line separated only by spaces
[1,2,3,,] is explicitly called invalid because it has two trailing commas
[,1,2,3] is explicitly called invalid because it has an initial comma
[1,,2,3] is explicitly called invalid because it has two commas in a row
these same comma rules apply to fields in objects, so two commas in a row between fields is invalid just as in an array
two fields need a comma or a newline between them; on one line with neither, 1 b becomes a value concatenation and the second = is a stray token
an initial comma is invalid in an object, the implicit root included
the array comma rules apply to object fields: two trailing commas are invalid
the array comma rules apply to object fields: an initial comma is invalid
when the substitutions turn out to be strings, the unquoted whitespace between them is significant and survives into the concatenated string
between substitutions that resolve to objects, unquoted whitespace is ignored but quoted whitespace should be an error
unquoted whitespace between substitutions that resolve to objects or lists must be ignored, so they merge and concatenate as if adjacent
whitespace between two list substitutions is ignored, tabs included, and the lists concatenate
U+00A0 is a Zs space and so whitespace in HOCON; between two list substitutions it is ignored (lightbend/config#862 review)
the BOM must be treated as whitespace, so between two list substitutions it is ignored
U+200B is format (Cf), not a space separator, so it is text, and text between two list substitutions is invalid. typesafe/config drops it and concatenates the lists; lightbend/config#862 rejects it
an undefined optional substitution in a concatenation with an array becomes an empty array

the mirror of 008: an undefined optional substitution before an array becomes an empty array too. typesafe/config keeps the whitespace before the list as text and rejects it, while accepting 008 (noted on lightbend/config#862)

merging objects loaded from different files is exactly the same behavior as merging duplicate fields in the same file: object-valued fields present in both files merge recursively and a non-object field takes the value from the later file

the spec's own example: an intermediate non-object value hides earlier object values because merging is done in pairs, so when 42 is paired with { y : 2 } it simply wins and loses all information about what it overrode, and the two objects are never merged
the spec's re-ordered example: with the non-object 42 moved to the lowest priority the two objects are adjacent, so they merge to { a : { x : 1, y : 2 } }
setting an object to null and then setting it back to a new object clears it and starts over, which is how to get rid of default fallback values from another file that you don't want

the spec's own example: an intermediate null is a non-object, so it replaces the first object and is in turn replaced by the second object with no merging, which prevents the two objects from ever seeing each other
only two object values merge; an array is not an object, so a later array replaces an earlier array (no concatenation) and replaces an earlier object (no merge)
null is a value like any other, so a later null overrides an earlier scalar or object: the key stays, set to null, rather than being removed or the assignment skipped

the null at r only stops merging at r; ${r} is the object {x:1}, and a later object merges with the earlier a, so helper stays. typesafe/config carries r's null through the substitution and drops helper (lightbend/config#864)
the same rule one level down: the null in v.nested's history belongs to v.nested, so a.nested still merges with the substituted {x:1} (lightbend/config#864)

a substitution sees the resolved value of the field it names, so o24bbd equals a.nested, which keeps helper. The key name is chosen to sort before a in typesafe/config's root HashMap, the order in which the first version of lightbend/config#864 answered differently for the two
the null belongs to v's history even when v's object is still unresolved, so a merges and keeps helper (lightbend/config#864)

v's value is a merge whose top is an object and whose null sits further down, under nested; that null is still v.nested's merge instruction, so a.nested keeps helper (lightbend/config#864 review, round 3)

two nested nulls each break only their own key's merge, and a lookup of a.n.d sees the final {x:1}; typesafe/config throws BugOrBroken in this key order (reported on lightbend/config#864, same on main)
four values for a, two of them substitutions that resolve to objects: all four merge in order
a string concatenation is a non-object value, so the later object replaces it rather than merging with it
the object layer of a's merge contains a field b that is itself a merge of a substitution and an object; both levels merge

the object replaces the earlier list, so a.m exists and p is 1 whatever order the keys are resolved in. typesafe/config fails when the reader p is resolved before a (it iterates p before a); the same file with the reader named zzz resolves
the same shape with a key the object does not have: the list below it is not consulted, a.b is undefined and the optional p is not created

a name without an extension is a basename: all of base.properties, base.json and base.conf exist, so all three are loaded and merged, properties first and HOCON last, so the .conf value wins where they overlap
a basename with only base.conf present loads just that file
a basename with only base.properties present loads it as Java properties, whose values are all strings
a basename that exists with no extension at all is a missing include, and a missing include is ignored
required() makes the missing basename an error

a file named .json is in JSON format, and an unquoted value is not JSON. typesafe/config parses a .json named outright with the HOCON parser, so the file is accepted; the same file found through a basename is rejected

a file named .properties is in Java properties format, where the first = separates key from value and values are strings. typesafe/config parses a .properties named outright with the HOCON parser and fails on the second =; the same file found through a basename is read as properties

in a properties file a dotted key is a path, so a.b and a.c build an object at a; the spec's Java properties mapping says the object must always win when a key is both a value and a parent, whatever the order; values are strings
a .json file found through a basename is parsed as JSON and contributes its object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an unquoted value is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; ${} is a HOCON extension, not JSON
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON has no trailing commas
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; the spec's own footing is that duplicate keys are invalid JSON (L194-195), so the second a is an error rather than an override
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON separates array elements with commas only; whitespace does not concatenate or separate
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; an empty document is not JSON, although it is an empty HOCON object
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON document included here must be an object; a bare number is neither an object nor valid as an included root
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a quoted string; a number cannot be a key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; in JSON a newline between fields does not stand in for the comma
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; a JSON key is a plain string, not a path expression, so a.b stays a single key
the .json file is found through a basename, so it is parsed as JSON; JSON forbids a leading zero on a number. typesafe/config reads 01 as 1, the same leniency it shows in HOCON

x.txt has an extension, so it is not a basename to probe; it is a file adjacent to the including one and of the same type. The spec does not define what counts as an extension, and this row reads any dotted suffix as one. typesafe/config probes every name that does not end in .conf, .json or .properties as a basename and finds nothing
base.properties and base.json both exist; JSON is parsed next-to-last, after properties, so its value for a wins
base.json and base.conf both exist; HOCON is parsed last, after JSON, so its value for a wins

a quoted include name with a known URL scheme is a URL, not a file adjacent to this one. With nothing behind the URL the include is ignored, so a parser that read the string as a filename would also get {}; the row records the rule, it cannot distinguish the two readings
inner.conf includes x.conf, which is found beside inner.conf, not beside main.conf and not in the process's working directory
x.conf is not a URL, so it names a file adjacent to main.conf
an absolute path is loaded as such, so the file of the same name beside main.conf is not it; the absolute file does not exist and the include is ignored
a file() argument is not interpreted relative to the including file, so the marker beside sub/inner.conf is not loaded; nothing of that name exists elsewhere and the include is ignored

the keys from the included object are conceptually substituted for the include statement in the including file, so the included field lands between the fields around it and merges by the usual duplicate-key rules
an included file must contain an object, not an array; if it contains an array as the root value it is invalid and an error should be generated
both JSON and HOCON allow arrays as root values in a document, but an included file must contain an object, so a JSON file with an array root is an error when included
the keys from the included root object are conceptually substituted for the include statement in the including file, so an include inside a nested object contributes its keys to that object

if a key in the included object occurred prior to the include statement in the including object, the included key's value overrides the earlier value, exactly as with duplicate keys found in a single file

if a key in the included object occurred prior to the include statement and both values are objects, the included value merges with the earlier value, exactly as with duplicate keys found in a single file
an included key's value overrides the earlier value exactly as with duplicate keys in a single file, so an included non-object replaces an earlier object rather than merging with it
if the including file repeats a key from an earlier-included object, the including file's value overrides the one from the included file
if the including file repeats a key from an earlier-included object and both values are objects, the including file's value merges with the one from the included file
an include statement may stand wherever a field may, including in an object that is a list element
the included file may contain substitutions like any other; typesafe/config refuses an include nested in a list when the included file is not fully resolved
the included file leaves a as an object merged with a substitution; that whole stack merges with the object the including file set earlier
the earlier value is itself a substitution; once everything resolves to objects, all three layers merge
the earlier value is a number, so the included object stack replaces it and merges only within itself
the same as 013 with the included stack the other way up, an object over a substitution; the result does not depend on which layer is on top
by default, if an included file does not exist the include statement is silently ignored, so the keys around it parse as if the line were not there
a missing include is treated as if the included file contained only an empty object, so an object whose only content is that include stays an empty object
the silent-ignore default applies to an explicit file() include as well: a file that does not exist contributes nothing and parsing continues
when the included resource name is wrapped with required(), file parsing fails with an error if the resource cannot be resolved
required() may also wrap the file() form, and a required file that cannot be resolved is a parse error rather than an empty object
required() only makes the include mandatory; a resource that does resolve is included exactly as an unwrapped include would be
a substitution in an included file must be fixed up to be relative to the app's configuration root, so ${x} in a file included at key a becomes ${a.x}
substitution happens after parsing the whole configuration, so the ${x} fixed up to ${a.x} evaluates to the root's later redefinition 42 rather than the included file's 10
it is not enough to only look up the fixed-up path; when a.x is undefined the original path x is looked up relative to the root of the including configuration
substitutions in included files are looked up first relative to the root of the included file and only second relative to the root of the including configuration, so a.x wins over x
only the fixed-up path a.x and the original path x are looked up; with neither defined the substitution is undefined and the configuration is invalid
an optional substitution in an included file is looked up at the fixed-up path a.x and at the original path x; with neither defined the field is omitted rather than an error
the fix-up is relative to the app's configuration root, so ${x} in a file included at b inside a file included at a becomes ${a.b.x}

an included file may intend to refer to the application's root config, for example to get a value from the environment; the original path CONFORMANCE_HOME is looked up and falls back to the environment variable

an undefined ${?nope} means common.x.y is never created, so ${x.y} is not found at the fixed-up path and is looked up at the original path x.y. typesafe/config treats the vanished value as a miss that ends the lookup -- except in some root key orders (see 014); lightbend/config#863 falls back
with neither common.x.y nor x.y defined, the required ${x.y} in the included file is unresolved
the optional form of 009 falls back the same way; typesafe/config leaves a out instead (lightbend/config#863)
an undefined optional that would override keeps the previous value, so common.x.y is 9 and found at the fixed-up path; the original path is not consulted
the metamorphic twin of 009 without the optional: common.x exists, common.x.y does not, so x.y is looked up at the original path
an unrelated key that reads common.x must not change what common.a resolves to; in typesafe/config this input fails while the same input with the key named o24bbd resolves to 0 (lightbend/config#863)
a substitution that is one piece of a concatenation in the included file is fixed up like a bare one: p.x is not set, so the original path x is used
a substitution that is a list element in the included file is fixed up as well
an object merged with a substitution in the included file keeps working after the fix-up, whichever of the two is on top: q is found at p.q
a.x is present, set to null, so the lookup at the fixed-up path succeeds and the original path x is not consulted

value concatenation is NOT performed on the argument to include; the argument must be a single quoted string, so a second quoted string after the resource name is an error whether or not the first resource exists

no substitutions are allowed in the argument to include, which must be a single quoted string; ${x} after include is an error even though x is defined, so an implementation that resolves the argument first still fails this row

if an unquoted include at the start of a key is followed by anything other than a single quoted string or the url()/file()/classpath() syntax, it is invalid and an error should be generated; the argument may not be an unquoted string
the argument inside file() must be a single quoted string; an unquoted name is a syntax error
file("...") must be closed; the line ends before the parenthesis
required(...) must be closed too
the string inside url() is always an absolute URL, with a scheme; x.conf has none, so it is an error, as lightbend/config#887 settled
any amount of whitespace, newlines included, may stand between include and the resource name
whitespace inside the parentheses, outside the quotes, is allowed
an unquoted include at the start of a key is never a key; followed by a separator instead of a quoted name it is an include with an invalid argument
an include stands where a field would, so the usual comma separates it from the field that follows
the separator may be omitted only before {; a key followed directly by [ is invalid
the [] suffix collects CONFORMANCE_LIST_0, CONFORMANCE_LIST_1, ... until an index is missing, into a list of strings
with no CONFORMANCE_LIST_0 set, an optional ${?X[]} is undefined and the field is not created
indices are collected from 0 until one is missing, so with _0 and _2 set the list holds only the first
an element taken from the environment is a string, so 1 stays "1"
the [] suffix collects environment variables only, so the config key a_0 is not gathered and the optional substitution is undefined
any sequence of at least three quotes ends the multi-line string and any extra quotes are part of the string, so HOCON works like Scala's four-character string foo" rather than Python's syntax error
a closing run of five quotes still only needs three to end the string, so both extra quotes are appended to the string value
a multi-line string opened with a three-character quote sequence that never reaches a closing """ is not a legal value
the conversion should be done in a concatenation when a list is expected and an object with numeric keys is found, so the trailing object concatenates onto the array as elements x, y
the conversion should ignore any keys which do not parse as positive integers, so key "foo" is dropped and only "0" contributes to the resulting array
the conversion should not occur if the object is empty, so an empty object cannot satisfy a list-expected concatenation and this is illegal
the conversion should not occur if the object has no keys which parse as positive integers, so this object cannot satisfy a list-expected concatenation and this is illegal

the conversion should sort by the integer value of each key and then build the array; missing indices such as "1" are eliminated rather than left as gaps, so keys "0" and "2" become a two-element array
the conversion ignores any keys which do not parse as positive integers, and "-1" is not a positive integer, so it is dropped and only key "0" contributes
the file does not begin with a bracket or brace, so it is wrapped in {} and becomes a key with no separator and no value

two arrays side by side concatenate when only non-newline whitespace separates them, which would make this document [1,2,3]; but a document is one array or one object at the root, and nothing in the spec lets a root value be a concatenation of two. typesafe/config, pyhocon and hocon-rs all reject it
the file does not begin with { or [, so it is read as if wrapped in braces, and a bare number there is a key with no value
a dot inside a quoted string has no special meaning as a path separator, so a quoted "a.b" key is a single-element path
foo.bar."hello.world" is a path with three elements: foo, bar, and hello.world, since unquoted dots are path separators but a quoted dot is not
foo followed by quoted "10.0" is an unquoted then a quoted string which concatenate, giving a single-element path
a path element that is an empty string must be quoted; a."".b is a valid three-element path whose middle element is the empty string
an unquoted empty path element is invalid, so a..b must generate an error
a path that starts with a dot is invalid and should generate an error
path expressions appear in substitutions as well as keys, and inside quoted strings a dot has no special meaning there either, so ${foo."bar.baz"} looks up key foo then the single key bar.baz
inside quotes a dot is not a separator, so ${"b.c"} names one field called b.c, which does not exist; it does not reach b's field c

the unquoted string include may not begin a path expression in a key: where an object key is expected, include is not read as a key at all and must be followed by a quoted resource name, so include.foo is an error. typesafe/config recognises the keyword only as a bare include token -- include.foo tokenizes as one unquoted string, so it is accepted as the path include.foo, while include = 42 is rejected under the very rule the spec states.
only the unquoted string include that begins a path expression in a key is special: include later in a key (foo.include) and a quoted "include" beginning one are ordinary path elements
a += b transforms into a = ${?a} [b], and because the fallback is optional (${?a} not ${a}) this is legal even as the first mention of a in the file
+= appends an element to a previous array
if the previous value was not an array, += results in an error just as the long form a = ${?a} [b] would with a non-array a
each += appends to the value the previous line left, so two of them append two elements
inside an object, += desugars to a self-reference by the field's full path o.a; the appended element may itself be a substitution
b has no previous value, so b += 1 is b = ${?b} [1] with the optional part undefined: [1]. typesafe/config refuses += inside a list because its desugared path cannot name a list element
the self-reference += desugars to uses the full path of the field, o.p.a, even when the enclosing key was written as the path o.p

l += v is l = ${?l} [v]; the appended object holds a merge of an object and a substitution, which resolves inside the new list. typesafe/config fails with an internal error (BugOrBroken) for the same reason as array-and-object-concatenation/018
in isolation, with no merges involved, a self-referential field is an error because the substitution cannot be resolved
when foo:${foo} is merged with an earlier value for foo, the self-reference resolves to that overridden value, so foo ends up { a : 1 }

if the self-referential foo:${foo} comes before foo has any value, the reference is undefined, exactly as if it named a path not found in the document, so it is an error even though foo is given a value afterward
because the self-reference error is treated as undefined rather than an intractable cycle, the optional syntax foo:${?foo} makes the field disappear silently instead of erroring
a self-reference resolves to the value below it even as part of a path expression, so ${foo.a} refers to { c : 1 } rather than 2, and the final merge is { a : 2, c : 1 }
an optional self-reference in a value concatenation has to look back to an undefined a, so a ends up "foo" rather than "foofoo"
the spec gives bar:${foo}, foo:${bar} as an example that is not possible to resolve, since neither lazy evaluation nor looking backward breaks the cycle and neither field is optional
a multi-step loop across three fields (a:${b}, b:${c}, c:${a}) must also be detected as invalid, not just a direct two-field cycle
the order a and b resolve in is undefined: both 1, both 2 or an error are all allowed, but a and b must agree (a=1,b=2 is not permitted)
a string concatenation is a non-object too, so it hides the earlier object (typesafe/config 1.4.5 evaluated it)
a substituted object merges with the earlier object, so its fields are part of the result and ${does-not-exist} is an error
a literal list is a non-object value, so it hides the earlier object and ${does-not-exist} is never evaluated
a genuine cycle is an error for required substitutions; with the optional syntax it is a missing value, so neither field is created
the text ${a} appears twice and resolves differently: to x in a's own self-reference and to the final xy in b; memoizing by path instead of by instance would give b the wrong value
a field may look up its own older value before being overridden with a new value based on it, letting path:${path}":d" extend the earlier path:"a:b:c"
a value concatenation containing a substitution to its own field is self-referential, so ${a} looks back to the earlier x and the result is xbc
the spec lists path:${path} [ /usr/bin ] among the examples of self-referential fields: a value concatenation of a substitution with an array literal is still self-referential
string value concatenation supports substitutions inside the concatenated string
it is invalid for arrays or objects to appear in a string value concatenation, since only simple values participate
whitespace before the first and after the last simple value is discarded; only the whitespace between the values is kept
string value concatenations never span a newline, so a bare word on the following line is not appended to the value above it
true and false become the strings "true" and "false" when they participate in a concatenation
null becomes the string "null" when it participates in a concatenation
numbers should be kept as they were originally written in the file when they participate in a concatenation, not renormalized

it is invalid for arrays or objects to appear in a string value concatenation; typesafe/config accepts this one silently and discards the trailing x, losing data with no diagnostic, while erroring on the same pair in the other order
the same rule for arrays; typesafe/config again accepts and discards the trailing x, where it errors when the scalar comes first
the same rule with the scalar first, which typesafe/config does reject -- the half of the rule it enforces
an array may not appear in a string value concatenation, with or without whitespace between them; typesafe/config silently drops suffix (lightbend/config#862)
the same rule for an object followed directly by text; typesafe/config silently drops suffix (lightbend/config#862)
text between two arrays makes a concatenation of array, string and array, which is invalid; typesafe/config drops the text and concatenates the arrays (lightbend/config#862)
a number in a concatenation is stringified as it appeared in the file, whatever its size
false becomes the string "false" in a concatenation, as true does
a quoted string is itself in a concatenation, and the whitespace between it and the unquoted string beside it is kept
a substitution whose path is not defined in the configuration falls back to an environment variable of the same name
a required ${x} substitution that is not present in the configuration tree is searched for in the environment and resolves to the variable's value instead of being an error
the lookup is case-sensitive all the way until the env variable fallback is reached, so a lowercase key does not shadow an uppercase substitution and the environment variable is used
an env variable set to the empty string is kept as such, so a required substitution resolves to "" rather than being undefined
an env variable set to the empty string is set to empty string rather than undefined, so an optional ${?x} substitution creates the field with "" instead of dropping it
environment variables always become a string value, so values that would parse as a number, a boolean or null in HOCON stay the strings "42", "true" and "null"
${?pathexpression} is the optional substitution syntax; when the path is defined it resolves exactly like ${pathexpression}, keeping the value and its type
substitutions are not parsed inside quoted strings, so this stays the literal text
worked example: to get a string containing a substitution, use value concatenation with the substitution in the unquoted portion
worked example: quoting the non-substitution portion also forms a value concatenation with the substitution
an undefined substitution with the ${foo} syntax is invalid and should generate an error
if an undefined ${?foo} substitution is the value of an object field, the field should not be created
if an undefined ${?foo} would override a previously-set value for the same field, the previous value remains
if an undefined ${?foo} substitution is an array element, the element should not be added
an undefined ${?foo} in a value concatenation with another string becomes an empty string
an undefined ${?foo} in a value concatenation with an object becomes an empty object
an undefined ${?foo} in a value concatenation with an array becomes an empty array
foo : ${?bar}${?baz} avoids creating the field only if both bar and baz are undefined
foo : ${?bar}${?baz} creates the field once at least one of bar or baz is defined
substitutions are only allowed in field values and array elements, not in keys
when a substitution is not the only part of a value, it is value-concatenated to form a string rather than keeping the substituted type

a substitution is undefined only if it does not match any value present in the configuration, and null is among the value types a substitution is replaced with, so ${?a} with a = null is defined: the field is created with null rather than omitted
a is a number, so a.x names nothing; a required substitution to an undefined path is an error
the same path with the optional form: undefined, so the field is not created
a substitution path has the syntax of an object key, so a quoted element may contain a space and names the field written the same way
an empty path element is legal when quoted, in a substitution as in a key

a path names object fields only, so b.0 does not reach into the list b even though it has an element at index 0; the optional substitution is undefined and a is not created. The list is still unresolved when the lookup happens, which is what makes an implementation look inside it
only whitespace before the ? is forbidden; after it the path follows and its leading whitespace is discarded as in any key

${?x}42 is a concatenation of two parts, so the value is a string: the undefined optional becomes empty and the number keeps its written form. The spec states the empty-string rule for a concatenation 'with another string', so this row extends it to a number; typesafe/config instead drops the undefined part and keeps the lone number as a number
quoted strings are in the same format as JSON strings, so JSON escapes like \n, \t, \", \\ and \u unicode escapes are honored
allowed number formats match JSON, including negative numbers, decimals, and exponent notation

allowed number formats match JSON, and JSON forbids a zero followed by further digits; the initial number character plus the valid-in-JSON number characters after it must be parsed as a number value, so the whole token 01 has to be a number and is not one, with no fallback offered. typesafe/config parses it leniently as the number 1.

allowed number formats match JSON, and JSON requires a digit before the decimal point, so -.33 is a number token that is not a valid number. typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -0.33; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) reads it as the unquoted string "-.33", like .33 -- still accepted, still not the error the hyphen rule asks for

the same JSON rule with an exponent: -.33e+1 has no integer part. typesafe/config releases up to 1.4.9 parse it as -3.3; upstream main since lightbend/config#861 (unreleased) rejects it, on the reserved +
JSON requires a digit after the decimal point; 1. is a number token that is not a valid number. typesafe/config reads it as 1, and lightbend/config#861 leaves it so on purpose
the same rule with an exponent after the dot; typesafe/config reads it as -1000 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)
JSON forbids leading zeros after the minus sign as well; typesafe/config reads it as -33 (named out of scope in lightbend/config#861)
the JSON escapes \/ \b \f and \r are valid in a quoted string and mean slash, backspace, form feed and carriage return
only the JSON escape sequences exist; \q is not one of them, so the string is invalid
\u must be followed by exactly four hex digits; zzzz are not hex digits
a quoted string that is still open at the end of the file is invalid
a backslash with nothing after it is not an escape and the string is still open at the end of the file
the file ends after two of the four hex digits a \u escape requires
JSON forbids unescaped control characters in strings, and a raw newline is one; a quoted string cannot span lines
a raw tab is a control character too, so it must be written as \t inside quotes
JSON writes a character outside the BMP as two \u escapes forming a surrogate pair, which decode to one character
quoted strings are JSON strings, and JSON's grammar accepts any \uXXXX escape, an unpaired surrogate included, so the string holds that one code unit
'@' is one of the listed forbidden characters, so it cannot appear inside an unquoted string
only the two-character string '//' is special for comments; a lone '/' is not a forbidden character and stays part of the unquoted string
backslash is a forbidden character, and unquoted strings support no escaping at all, so a literal backslash requires a quoted string instead

an unquoted string may not begin with a hyphen, and the initial number character plus any valid-in-JSON number characters that follow must be parsed as a number value -- here that is the lone '-', which is not a number. typesafe/config falls back to unquoted text and yields the string '-foo', the same leniency it shows for '1e'.
some forbidden characters, such as '!', have no meaning in HOCON today and are reserved as keywords for future extensions to the spec
quoted JSON strings may not contain control characters, per the JSON spec, unlike unquoted strings
+ is a forbidden character in an unquoted string and outside quotes only forms the += separator; a + with nothing after it, here at the end of the file, is invalid
1+2 begins like a number and is not one; + is a forbidden character, so the token cannot fall back to an unquoted string either
1e begins with a digit, so the run of number characters 1e must be parsed as a number, and it is not one; typesafe/config falls back to the unquoted string "1e", the same leniency it shows for -foo
unquoted strings support no escaping, so \u00e9 is not decoded, and the backslash it needs is forbidden in an unquoted string; the quoted "caf\u00e9" is how to write it

an unquoted string may not begin with the digits 0-9, and the initial number character plus any valid-in-JSON number characters that follow it must be parsed as a number value -- 1.2.3 is that run, and it is not a number, so the input is rejected rather than read as a string (the everyday shape is an address like 127.0.0.1); typesafe/config and pyhocon both fall back to the unquoted string "1.2.3"
if all the values are simple values they are concatenated into a string
a nonbreaking space (0x00A0) is a Unicode Zs separator and must be treated as whitespace
vertical tab (0x000B) and form feed (0x000C) are whitespace characters
the spec names figure space (0x2007) and narrow no-break space (0x202F) explicitly among the nonbreaking spaces treated as whitespace
a lone carriage return is whitespace but not a newline, so 1 b concatenates and the second = is a stray token
U+2028 around the separator is whitespace, not part of the key or the value
the file, group, record and unit separators 0x1C-0x1F are whitespace around keys and separators
the ideographic space U+3000 is a Zs space separator and so whitespace, like every member of the category
the BOM is whitespace wherever it appears, not only as a file-start marker
